newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Dublin, Sinn Fein urge unionists to stay in talks.
newsitem.headline: Dublin, Sinn Fein urge unionists to stay in talks.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern met the head of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing on Friday, marking the restart of direct contacts after a new guerrilla ceasefire in British-ruled Northern Ireland.

Ahern, Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams and moderate nationalist leader John Hume jointly urged Northern Ireland's pro-British unionists to back a struggling talks initiative aimed at ending decades of strife with pro-Irish republicans.
"We recognise that ultimately we can resolve this problem only with the participation and agreement of the unionist people," the three leaders said in a statement which Ahern read to journalists.

Adams and Hume had an hour of talks with Ahern in Dublin, five days after the Irish Republican Army called off its armed campaign against British rule to secure a place for Sinn Fein in all-party peace talks.

Friday's meeting was a major step out of the political wilderness for Sinn Fein, ending a freeze on direct ministerial contacts imposed by Dublin after the IRA set off bombs in London in February 1996 to end a previous ceasefire.

Britain is also expected to resume direct contact with Sinn Fein soon in response to the ceasefire, which has been in force since last Sunday. Political sources in Belfast said Sinn Fein leaders might meet British ministers next week.

However, the peace process was jolted on Wednesday when two Protestant unionist parties stormed out, accusing London of pandering to republican hardliners by letting them join talks without a commitment to disarm.
The main Ulster Unionist Party, led by David Trimble, shares this view but says it will remain in the talks process.

Ahern hoped London and Dublin could persuade the unionists, who speak for Northern Ireland's majority Protestants, to stay in the talks -- which Sinn Fein will be allowed to join on September 15 if the IRA ceasefire is judged genuine.

"It is very important that the two governments remain in the driving seat. I hope we can find a way to give satisfactory bona fides to the unionists and Trimble to get them to come to the September 15 talks," Ahern said.
Adams said all sides must be there. "All sides have equal rights and deserve equal treatment."
Hume, leader of Northern Ireland's Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party, has played a major role in trying to bridge the gulf between republicans and Britain.
"Already the atmosphere is significantly improved. Our challenge is to build on the positive and get all the parties around the table on September 15," Hume told reporters.
Trimble said his decision not to follow others in storming out of talks had thwarted IRA hopes that unionists would portray themselves as intransigent.
"That is what the Provos (IRA) were setting up. It was obvious they were trying to wrong-foot unionists with their ceasefire," he told the Belfast News Letter in an interview.
